title: Opened Is Not Fixed: The Last Mile of AI Vulnerability Remediation
thesis: With AI making vulnerability discovery cheap, the bottleneck is patching, and AI-written fixes that pass their own tests often leave variants open, so a fix validation loop must include an independent variant hunt before a finding is closed.
summary: Shayaun Nejad draws on Rubrik's participation in Project Glasswing, where Anthropic gave early access to find bugs in Rubrik's own systems. He says the ratio inverted: finding bugs got easy, and patching became the constraint, pulling top engineers off the product roadmap, much as Bank of America reportedly brought in 1,000 contractors. The main problem was that bugs marked fixed kept coming back, either as variants next to the original or when a stronger model arrived. He illustrates with a public case, the vm2 JavaScript sandbox package: a critical advisory fixed with a commit co-authored by Claude and 28 passing tests, which he bypassed during slide preparation with a one-line change to which file endings the sandbox trusts, shown in a recorded demo that exfiltrates a synthetic host token. He cites a P2Patch preprint finding that 41 of 101 AI-patched CVEs had variants. Rubrik runs separate scanning, validation and patching pipelines and added a variant-hunt stage after tests pass, with recurring variants routed to a human. He also classifies bugs by whether they can be auto-patched, keeps a unified vulnerability record so new models can reopen fixes, uses recurring bug classes to direct investment (fuzzing for memory errors, design-phase work for logic bugs), and notes Rubrik productized the harness as Code Guardian. His one takeaway is to build variant analysis into hunting and patching pipelines.
argument: Discovery has become cheap, so the backlog and patching capacity are now the constraint, and engineering time shifts from product work to remediation.
AI-generated fixes are validated by AI-written tests, so a passing test suite shows only that the known exploit is blocked, not that the root cause is fixed.
Fixed bugs reopen as variants, either from the same weak spot or neighbors, and when a stronger model or chained lower-severity issue arrives.
Published advisories and security commits are a source-to-sink map for attackers, so defenders must hunt variants of their own fixes first.
Add an explicit variant hunt after tests pass, classify which fixes are safe to auto-patch, keep history for re-evaluation under new models, and use recurring bug classes to direct investment.

frameworks.name: Variant hunt in fix validation
frameworks.description: Before: fix, tests pass, closed. After: fix, tests pass, variant hunt, then if any variant, fix and retest, otherwise close.

frameworks.name: Variant sweep loop
frameworks.description: Fix feeds a variant sweep, which finds misses; recurring variants go to a human; a new model feeds into the sweep and can reopen any fix. Each variant caught makes the next sweep smaller.

frameworks.name: Separated security agent pipelines
frameworks.description: Distinct pipelines for vulnerability scanning, validation, patching, then back to validation, with variant analysis added as its own agentic hunt after patching.

frameworks.name: KNighter-style variant brief
frameworks.description: Chain on a slide: fix, rule, nearby mistake, impact, test. Input is a published fix plus adjacent source; the model is asked for a rule, a candidate, a potential impact, and a check.

vm2 advisory screenshot: Critical severity, GitHub Reviewed, published Sep 8, affected versions <= 3.12.1, patched 3.12.2; commit fb4977f by patriksimek-bot and claude, message fix(GHSA-5h3f-q97h-ccvc): boundary-match custom-resolver authorizations, Tests: test/ghsa/GHSA-5h3f-q97h-ccvc/repro.js (28 cases), Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1.

Source-to-sink slide lists code locations in vm2: lib/nodevm.js 516-575, lib/resolver.js 227-316, lib/resolver-compat.js 266-291, 193-215 (isPathAllowedForModule falls back to a regex whose dynamically appended expression also matches sibling paths such as foo2 because no path separator or end-of-string is required) and 255-263 (loadJS uses hostRequire for host-context files and wraps exports only with vm.readonly, so top-level effects occur in the host process).

Terminal slide: commit fb4977f changed 5 files, 681 insertions and 33 deletions, mostly lib/resolver-compat.js (211) and test repro.js (414). A public-brief.txt gives the KNighter chain (fix, rule, nearby mistake, impact, test) with input of published fix plus adjacent source and app of custom resolver, host context, adjacent uploaded file. A Claude invocation with no tools returned: RULE approve one exact file and only from endings the host controls; CANDIDATE script-chosen file endings could approve a lookalike upload; POTENTIAL upload runs on the server and could leak passwords and customer files; CHECK try adding an ending in a test, then lock the list to fixed values.

Demo slide steps: the guest code tries to require an unlisted file ending in -preview.js and is blocked with ENOTFOUND, and no credential is received at the sink. The variant adds one line, require.extensions['-preview.js'] = require.extensions['.js'], after which the host process sent the token. Captioned Reported privately to the maintainer.

Slide terminal session in which Claude is run with no tools against a variant brief built from the published fix, producing a rule, candidate, potential impact and check for the bypass.

offense: Variant analysis against a published fix: feed the advisory, the fix commit and adjacent source to a model and ask for the rule the fix enforced, the nearby mistake, the impact and a test.

vm2 bypass: the fix constrained custom-resolver authorizations by file ending; a one-line change to which endings the sandbox trusts let a guest load an unlisted file in the host context and leak a host token.
Advisories name source-to-sink paths with file and line ranges, which gives an adversarial model the best possible context.
A stronger model or chaining of lower-severity issues can reopen a bug previously marked fixed.
defense: Add a variant-hunt stage after tests pass and before closing a vulnerability; if a variant is found, fix and retest.
Keep scanning, validation and patching as separate pipelines or agents, and return patches to validation.
Classify each finding by whether it can be auto-patched or needs a human; simple classes such as SQL injection can be auto-patched, authentication bypass and architectural issues need review.
Keep a unified vulnerability record so past fixes can be re-examined whenever a new model is adopted.
Route recurring variants to a human and track recurring bug classes to direct investment (fuzzing, design-phase review).
Rely on extensive CI/CD with unit tests and security checks at the pull request stage, adding tests as breakages occur.
Run chaining analysis and escalate lower-severity issues that chain to critical; avoid blind patching of mediums and lows.
Be careful what you disclose in advisories and commit messages, since they disclose the vulnerability classes your platform is susceptible to.
takeaways: Change the definition of done for a vulnerability from patch merged and tests pass to variant hunt clean, and track opened, reviewed and fixed as separate states.
Treat AI-written fixes validated by AI-written tests as unverified; require an independent variant sweep, ideally with a different prompt or model than the patcher.
Classify findings by auto-patchability and send authentication, authorization and architectural issues to a human reviewer first.
Re-run variant sweeps on closed findings when you adopt a stronger model, and keep the history that makes that possible.
Audit what your own advisories and security commits reveal before publishing, because attackers will use them as variant-hunting context.
limits: Speaker said he cannot disclose the types or number of bugs found in Rubrik's code.
Variant analysis is not perfect and hallucination risk exists at every LLM step; stronger models give better results.
Only the top severity findings could be fixed because of volume; lower severities were prioritized by chain analysis.
Before classification was added, AI-generated patches at volume could pass unit tests and reach production.
critique: The Rubrik evidence is qualitative: no counts of reopened fixes, variant rates, patch success before versus after, or time to close, so the claim that variant analysis improved success is unsupported by numbers.

The vm2 example is persuasive as a demo but shows one bypass; it does not measure how common such bypasses are across AI-written fixes, and the 41 of 101 figure comes from a single preprint not described in detail.
The vm2 commit co-author count differs between speech (15) and slide (19), the slide figure is the one recorded.

The speaker works for Rubrik, which offers Code Guardian, a product built on this harness. The recommended practice (add a variant stage) applies an existing technique, variant analysis, to the patching pipeline, and the talk did not address which model finds variants if the same model wrote the fix.
The Q&A shows classification was by simple heuristics and a decision model whose details were not given, so the escalation design is hard to reproduce.
qa: Question on validating that a fix works and does not break anything: Rubrik relies on an extensive CI/CD pipeline with many unit tests, adds tests as needed, and classifies bugs by type, using simple heuristics before (SQL injection easily patched; authentication bypass needs a human) so risky fixes get a human in the loop.

Question on how variants are generated: pass the threat model and historical vulnerabilities to an LLM and have it generate variants; with a capable model you can point it at a repo and ask it to hunt for bypasses of the advisory and security-fix commits.

Question on how a decision model was used in triage: the classifier decided which fixes needed more human resourcing, so complex versions of an otherwise easy class such as SQL injection went to a human; the speaker described it as escalation classification and said they were also trying it in the SDLC. The model name is garbled in the transcript.
Question on whether the sloppy patches improved: the patches were AI-generated at volume and could pass tests into production, which motivated adding classification and a better process.
Question on whether all severities were fixed: only the top ones, because volume was too high; all the scary ones were handled.
Challenge that low severities chain: agreed, Rubrik runs chaining analysis and patches lower severities when chains escalate to critical, rather than blindly patching all mediums and lows.
